faqs.question: Do deaf people in India and America use the same signs?
faqs.answer: No. ISO 639-3 registers Indian Sign Language as ins and American Sign Language as ase — separate individual living languages with separate lexicons. A sign learned from an ASL dictionary will not be understood as Indian Sign Language.

faqs.question: What is the ASL sign for miss?
faqs.answer: ASL-LEX 2.0 records it as entry G_02_049, SignBank gloss MISS, with the English translations disappointed, miss, pine for and yearn for. It is coded as a “1” handshape at the chin, one-handed, with contact and no path movement. Watch the entry's video rather than working from that description.

faqs.question: Is the ASL sign for miss made at the nose or the chin?
faqs.answer: ASL-LEX 2.0 codes it MajorLocation Head, MinorLocation Chin. Only 101 of the database's 2,723 signs (3.7%) are coded at the chin, and MISS is one of them — so pages that place it at the nose are describing something else.

faqs.question: Does 🤟 mean I miss you?
faqs.answer: No. The ILY handshape is ASL-LEX entry F_01_102, SignBank gloss I-LOVE-YOU, and its listed translations are “I love you, ILY, love”. Unicode names the emoji U+1F91F “love-you gesture”. Miss is not one of its meanings.

faqs.question: What is the difference between MISS and MISSING in ASL?
faqs.answer: They are unrelated signs. ASL-LEX codes MISS (G_02_049) at the chin as a one-handed sign, while the entry English calls missing is E_02_017, whose SignBank gloss is GONE — depleted, empty, gone, pass away, used up. English collapses two meanings into one word; ASL does not.

faqs.question: Why do sign language guides keep telling me to watch a video?
faqs.answer: Because signs are movement and prose cannot specify one. ASL-LEX gives MISS a phonological neighbourhood density of 50 — the highest of all 2,723 signs, against a median of 3 — and two other signs, SERIOUS and the sign glossed BITTER, carry values identical to it on every coded field.

faqs.question: How do I say I miss you in Indian Sign Language?
faqs.answer: Look it up in the ISLRTC dictionary and watch it. The Indian Sign Language Research and Training Centre publishes the national ISL dictionary as video — a dictionary website, a YouTube channel, a Drive folder and an open dataset — with no text entry carrying phonological coding, so no honest written description exists to reproduce.

faqs.question: How do I say I miss you in British Sign Language?
faqs.answer: BSL SignBank returns two signs for the English word miss, and neither means longing. One is keyworded disappointment, disappoint, disappointed, miss; the other miss, err, error, mistake, wrong, misunderstand. Searches for longing, yearn, absent and want return nothing at all.

faqs.question: Do I have to make the facial expression, or is the hand enough?
faqs.answer: The face is part of the grammar, not decoration. Wiktionary's ASL entries write it into the production description itself — the entry for ANGRY opens “produced with an angry scowl” — and a 2026 PLOS ONE production experiment on Dutch Sign Language found non-manual marking distinguishing question forms.

faqs.question: Is it okay for a hearing person to use a sign in a message?
faqs.answer: If both of you are hearing, it is borrowing someone's working language as an ornament, and that is worth not doing. If your recipient is Deaf or signs, learning the sign from their own language's dictionary and filming yourself is the point of the exercise.

article.contentMarkdown:
# I Miss You in Sign Language: Which One, and Why It Needs Video

There is no single "sign language", so there is no single answer. In American Sign Language the sign glossed MISS — the one whose dictionary translations are *pine for* and *yearn for* — is recorded in the [ASL-LEX 2.0 lexical database](https://asl-lex.org/) as a "1" handshape at the **chin**, one-handed, with contact and no path movement. British Sign Language is a different language, and [UCL's BSL SignBank](https://bslsignbank.ucl.ac.uk/dictionary/search/?query=miss) returns two entries for the English word *miss*, neither of which means longing for someone. Indian Sign Language has its own national dictionary from ISLRTC, and it is published as video, not text. Of the 214 "I miss you" pages built on SubhSandesh's /missyou-gf template since 2026-07-28, 13.6% carry a voice note — the one field on that page a Deaf recipient cannot use. Below: which sign belongs to which language, what each database actually records, and why the last step has to be a video.

## "Sign language" is not one language

A signed language is a full natural language with its own vocabulary, grammar and history, carried in the visual-manual channel rather than the vocal one. There is no universal version, and there never was.

The international standard says so plainly. [ISO 639-3](https://iso639-3.sil.org/code/ase) registers American Sign Language, British Sign Language, Indian Sign Language, Dutch Sign Language, French Sign Language and Auslan under six separate codes — `ase`, `bfi`, `ins`, `dse`, `fsl`, `asf` — each classed Individual and Living. Six codes, six languages.

ASL and BSL are not mutually intelligible and are not even related. ASL fingerspells on one hand, BSL on two. So "how do you say I miss you in sign language" is the same shape of question as "how do you say it in European", and every sign below is labelled with its language.

## Six entries, six named languages and databases

ASL-LEX 2.0 is a lexical database of 2,723 American Sign Language signs, each coded on handshape, location, movement and contact. Its public data file was parsed for this article, so every ASL value below is the database's own. For each entry: the language, what the database records, and what it does not mean.

### 1. ASL — MISS, entry code G_02_049

ASL-LEX records this under the SignBank gloss MISS, translations "disappointed, miss, pine for, yearn for". The coding: handshape "1" (index finger, fully open, thumb closed), one-handed, major location Head, **minor location Chin**, contact present, movement "None", duration 834 ms.

This is the sign people mean when they search this phrase. Thirty-two raters scored it 2.875 of 7 for iconicity against the prompt "TO MISS SOMEONE", and ASL-LEX classes it **Arbitrary**: it does not look like its meaning, so guessing it from a photo fails.

### 2. ASL — GONE, the sign English calls "missing", entry code E_02_017

A different sign entirely. Its SignBank gloss is GONE, translations "depleted, empty, gone, missing, pass away, used up".

It is asymmetrical with two handshapes, located at the Palm and moving away from the hand, no contact — nothing in common with G_02_049. English uses *missing* for both "I miss you" and "the keys are missing"; ASL does not.

### 3. ASL — LONELY, entry code B_03_078, one parameter away

LONELY is coded with the same handshape "1" at the same location, Head/Chin, with contact — identical to MISS except that it has straight, repeated movement where MISS has none.

Its translations are "all alone, alone, lonely, lonesome". Two signs a written description renders almost identically are different words, and motion is what separates them.

### 4. ASL — I-LOVE-YOU, the 🤟 handshape, entry code F_01_102

The ILY handshape combines the fingerspelled I, L and Y — ASL-LEX flags it `Initialized = 1`, built from letters. Its SignBank gloss is I-LOVE-YOU, translations "I love you, ILY, love".

**"Miss" is not among them.** Unicode names the matching emoji U+1F91F "love-you gesture", from Emoji 5.0. It is one-handed, repeated straight movement in neutral space, no contact — different from MISS on every coded parameter. Send 🤟 meaning "I miss you" and you have said something else.

### 5. BSL — the two entries SignBank returns for "miss"

UCL's BSL SignBank is the reference database for British Sign Language. Searching *miss* returns "4 full or partial matches", and the two signs behind it carry these keyword sets:

**miss-1:** disappointment, disappoint, disappointed, miss. **miss-2:** miss, err, error, mistake, wrong, misunderstand, misunderstanding. **Neither means "to long for someone."**

*Longing*, *yearn*, *absent* and *want* return no entry at all. SignBank publishes video and no written form description, so none is reproduced here.

### 6. ISL — what ISLRTC publishes, and what this page will not describe

Indian Sign Language has a national dictionary from the [Indian Sign Language Research and Training Centre](https://islrtc.nic.in/isl-dictionary/), a body under the Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities, established 28 September 2015 after a campaign by India's Deaf community.

The dictionary is distributed as video — a website, a YouTube channel, a Drive folder and an open dataset released under NDSAP by the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment. **There is no text entry with phonological coding, so this page prints no ISL description of "I miss you".** Go and watch it. ISLRTC's own statement of need cites the 2011 Census figure of about 50 lakh deaf people in India; a query this Indian deserves the Indian dictionary, not a footnote.

## Is there one sign for "I miss you"? No, and the face is part of the grammar

None of the three databases consulted lists a single lexical sign meaning "I miss you". What exists is a construction — a pronoun, the verb, a pointing reference to the addressee — plus non-manual marking on the face, head and body.

Non-manual markers are grammar, not expression. A production experiment on Dutch Sign Language [published open-access in PLOS ONE on 29 July 2026](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0354015) found that NGT polar questions differ by polarity marking, question tags and non-manual marking — and that, contrary to what the previous literature predicted, raised eyebrows are *not* consistently used. The authors propose a head or body forward position as the main marker instead.

The lexicon shows it too. [Wiktionary's ASL entries](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Claw5@NearNose-PalmBack) write the face into the production description: ANGRY begins "This one-handed ASL sign is produced with an angry scowl", and the entry glossed DON'T-MIND is "usually made while twisting the head from side to side". The face is part of the word, not styling.

## A written description of a sign is not a sign

ASL-LEX records a phonological neighbourhood density for every entry — how many other signs sit one parameter change away. Across all 2,723 signs the median is 3 and the mean 5.0.

**MISS scores 50, the highest value in the entire database**, ahead of seven signs tied at 47. The sign this article is about is the most confusable one ASL-LEX has measured.

Fourteen signs are coded with a "1" handshape at the chin, and two — SERIOUS and the sign glossed BITTER, "bitter, disappoint, nasty, sour, yucky" — carry values identical to MISS on every phonological field. Three words, one coded form, because the differences live in movement, timing and the face. Treat any written description, including the ones above, as a label for finding the right video, never as instructions for producing the sign.

## How to actually send it, compared

These are the measured fields on SubhSandesh's miss-you pages, n = 214 over the two months since the template went live on 2026-07-28 — too short for a seasonal claim, too small for a per-city rate.

| Channel on a miss-you page | Works for a Deaf recipient | Can carry a sign correctly | Used by senders, n = 214 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Written letter | Yes | No — prose cannot specify movement | Every page; median 88 words, longest 1,024 |
| Voice note | No — audio only | No | 13.6% (29 of 214) |
| Reunion countdown | Yes | Not applicable | 28.0% (60 of 214) |
| Recipient "hug" tap | Yes | Not applicable | 1,434 taps across 138 of 214 pages |
| Video of you signing | Yes | Yes — the only format that can | Not a field measured on the template |

The takeaway is the bottom row: the only channel that carries a sign is the one the template does not have. Film it and give it a page — a [video page built for one person](/watch), with chapters and a pinned comment, fits a message that has to move.

## When a signed message is the wrong thing to send

If you and your partner are both hearing, borrowing a sign for a caption is not what these languages are for. ISL and ASL are the working languages of Deaf communities, and using one as decoration is a small unkindness dressed as a sweet idea. Send words in a language you both use.

If your recipient is Deaf, the honest ranking puts SubhSandesh second. Learn the sign from their language's dictionary, film yourself, send that. A [miss-you page](/missyou-gf) is a good frame around the video and a good home for the letter — the median one runs 88 words — but it is the frame, not the message.

Two limits on the numbers above. The 2,417 recorded views across those pages are page views, not unique visitors, so one person reopening a page twenty times reads as twenty.

And the 47 city pairs the pages name come from a 15-city picker with a default, so they describe the picker as much as the senders; the genuinely chosen fields are the password, the voice note, the reunion date, the letter, the memories and the open-when letters. On the first of those, miss-you senders are the most private segment measured here: 43.5% password-protect the page, against 38.5% platform-wide.

For the spoken versions of this phrase, the [I miss you in different languages hub](/blog/i-miss-you-in-different-languages) covers 50-plus. That hub is spoken languages only; this page is its one signed entry, which is a different kind of language and needs a different kind of answer.

## Sources

- [ASL-LEX 2.0](https://asl-lex.org/) — Sevcikova Sehyr, Caselli, Cohen-Goldberg & Emmorey; 2,723 ASL signs. Data file parsed for codes G_02_049, E_02_017, B_03_078, F_01_102.
- [ISO 639-3 registry](https://iso639-3.sil.org/code/ase) — SIL International; separate codes `ase`, `bfi`, `ins`, `dse`, `fsl`, `asf`.
- [BSL SignBank, UCL DCAL](https://bslsignbank.ucl.ac.uk/dictionary/search/?query=miss) — the two BSL entries returned for *miss*.
- Oomen, Esselink & Roelofsen, ["Polar questions in Dutch Sign Language (NGT)"](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0354015), *PLOS ONE* 21(7): e0354015, 29 July 2026.
- [ISLRTC](https://islrtc.nic.in/isl-dictionary/) — Indian Sign Language Dictionary, Government of India.
- [Wiktionary ASL entries](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Claw5@NearNose-PalmBack) — production descriptions that include non-manual markers.

sources.stat: ASL-LEX 2.0, a lexical database of 2,723 American Sign Language signs with phonological coding (Sevcikova Sehyr, Caselli, Cohen-Goldberg & Emmorey). The public data file behind the visualisation, https://asl-lex.org/visualization/data/sign_props.json, was fetched and parsed in full in this session: 2,723 records. Entry `miss` (Code G_02_049): Handshape "1", SelectedFingers "i", Flexion FullyOpen, ThumbPosition Closed, SignType OneHanded, Movement None, RepeatedMovement 0, MajorLocation Head, MinorLocation Chin, Contact 1, SignDuration 834 ms, SignFrequency(M) 5.423 (N=27), Iconicity(M) 2.875 (N=32) type Arbitrary against the prompt "TO MISS SOMEONE", SignBankAnnotationID MISS, SignBankEnglishTranslations "disappointed, miss, pine for, yearn for", Neighborhood Density 50. Entry `missing` (E_02_017): SignBank gloss GONE, translations "depleted, empty, gone, missing, pass away, used up". Entry `lonely` (B_03_078): same handshape and Head/Chin location as miss, differing only in Straight repeated movement. Entry `I_love_you` (F_01_102): Handshape "ily", Initialized = 1, SignBank gloss I-LOVE-YOU, translations "I love you, ILY, love". Computed directly from the file: 101 of 2,723 signs (3.7%) coded MinorLocation Chin; neighbourhood density median 3, mean 5.0, maximum 50 held by `miss` alone, with seven signs tied at 47; 14 signs coded handshape 1 at Head/Chin, of which `serious` (B_01_071) and `sour` (F_03_060, gloss BITTER) match `miss` on every phonological field. Cap-exempt reference instrument per capcheck. The site publishes no date.

ISO 639-3 registry, SIL International (registration authority). Code pages fetched for ase American Sign Language, bfi British Sign Language, ins Indian Sign Language, dse Dutch Sign Language, fsl French Sign Language and asf Auslan (Australian Sign Language). Each is listed Status Active, Scope Individual, Language Type Living — six separate individual living languages, which is the primary-standard proof that "sign language" is not one language. Cap-exempt reference instrument. The registry publishes no per-entry date.

BSL SignBank, UCL Deafness Cognition and Language Research Centre. A search for "miss" returns "4 full or partial matches" (miss, missile, missionary, missioner). The two signs reached from miss carry these keyword sets, read from the entry pages: /dictionary/words/miss-1.html — "disappointment, disappoint, disappointed, miss"; /dictionary/words/miss-2.html — "miss, err, error, mistake, wrong, misunderstand, misunderstanding". Neither carries a "long for someone" sense. Searches for longing, yearn, absent and want return no entry; lonely returns two and love returns two. Each entry publishes a video and no written form description. Fetched in this session; the site publishes no date.

Oomen, M., Esselink, L. & Roelofsen, F., "Polar questions in Dutch Sign Language (NGT): A production experiment", PLOS ONE 21(7): e0354015. Peer-reviewed, open access (CC-BY); the article page was fetched and the abstract read in full. The study identifies a range of NGT polar question forms differing in polarity marking, presence of question tags and use of non-manual markers, and reports that, contrary to expectation given the previous literature on polar questions in sign languages, raised eyebrows are not consistently used — brow lowering is also common — leading the authors to suggest that a head or body forward position, not raised eyebrows, is the main polar question marker in NGT. Received 2025-10-17, accepted 2026-07-02, published 2026-07-29. Full text is open; only the abstract was relied on for the figures quoted.

Indian Sign Language Research and Training Centre (ISLRTC), Government of India. The ISL Dictionary page was fetched: the dictionary is distributed as video via a dictionary website, a YouTube channel, a Google Drive folder and an open dataset on data.gov.in (catalog page also fetched — contributor Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment / Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities, released under the National Data Sharing and Accessibility Policy, Published On 07/02/2024, Updated On 18/02/2025). No text entry with phonological coding is published, so no ISL sign is described in this post. The centre's About page (islrtc.nic.in/about-department/about-islrtc/, Publish Date July 8, 2024) records ISLRTC's establishment on 28 September 2015 as a Society under DEPwD, MSJE, and states: "As per the 2011 Census, the total population of deaf persons in India numbered about 50 lakh." That Census figure is this post's single generic context statistic. Cap-exempt reference instrument per capcheck.

English Wiktionary ASL entry, title in sign notation, gloss ANGRY. Its Production section opens: "This one-handed ASL sign is produced with an angry scowl" — the non-manual marker is written into the lexical entry itself. Also fetched: 1@Nose-FingerBack 1@FromNose-FingerForward (gloss DON'T-MIND), whose production note specifies it is "usually made while twisting the head from side to side (the typical “no” headshake)"; Y@InsideChesthigh-PalmDown Sidetoside (SAME-AS), carrying Stokoe notation ØY≿; and the English entry `miss`, which separates the noun sense "a failure to physically hit" from verb sense 11 "to become aware of the loss or absence of… to feel sadness at the absence of somebody". A full-text search of Wiktionary for an ASL entry glossed MISS returns nothing — Wiktionary's ASL coverage is about a hundred lemmas and MISS is not among them, which is why the ASL claims here rest on ASL-LEX. Cap-exempt reference instrument. Wiktionary publishes no per-entry date.

structuralLimitations: THE TASK PROMPT'S CENTRAL ANATOMICAL CLAIM IS WRONG, AND THE DATABASE SAYS SO. The prompt instructed: "The ASL sign for MISS (the one made at the nose)". ASL-LEX 2.0 codes entry `miss` (G_02_049) as MajorLocation Head, MinorLocation **Chin** — not Nose. The file was fetched and parsed in this session; a direct count over all 2,723 records gives 101 signs (3.7%) coded at the chin, matching the entry's own MinorLocation.2.0Frequency of 0.037. The post states the chin, the H1 promise rests on it, and the prompt's framing was discarded rather than built on. This is the BRIEF §0 check working as intended.

THE CENTRAL CLAIM IS MEASURED FROM A STANDARDS REGISTRY, NOT ASSERTED. "Sign language is not one language" is proved from ISO 639-3 itself: six code pages were fetched (ase, bfi, ins, dse, fsl, asf) and each reads Status Active, Scope Individual, Language Type Living. Indian Sign Language holds its own code `ins`, distinct from `ase` and `bfi`. That is the same standard of proof the sibling post miss-you-emoji-meaning set with Unicode's emoji-test.txt.

THE CONFUSABILITY FINDING IS COMPUTED, AND IT IS THE POST'S BEST CLAIM. ASL-LEX's Neighborhood Density 2.0 field was read for all 2,723 records: median 3, mean 5.0, maximum 50 — and 50 belongs to `miss` alone, ahead of seven signs tied at 47 (humble, promise, blood, tomato, true_business, plain, dedicate_1). Separately, 14 signs are coded handshape "1" at Head/Chin, and two of them — `serious` (B_01_071) and `sour` (F_03_060, SignBank gloss BITTER) — carry values identical to `miss` on every phonological field in the database, while `lonely` (B_03_078) differs only in movement. Three unrelated meanings, one coded form. That is the measured version of "a still description is not a sign", and nothing on the SERP carries it.

SIGNS I REFUSED TO DESCRIBE, AND WHY. (1) The ASL sign for MISS meaning "failed to catch" — ASL-LEX 2.0 contains no entry for that sense; the only neighbouring entry is `missing` (E_02_017) whose gloss is GONE. Since I could not source the catch sign to a named dictionary, the post does not describe it and says the two senses are unrelated using GONE instead, which IS sourced. (2) Any ISL form for "I miss you" — ISLRTC publishes the national dictionary as video only, with no text entry carrying phonological coding, and the dictionary's own host divyangjan.depwd.gov.in timed out on two attempts from this session. The reader is sent to ISLRTC rather than given an invented description. (3) Any BSL form description — BSL SignBank publishes video and keyword sets, not written form descriptions, so only the keyword sets are quoted. (4) Any single lexical sign meaning "I miss you" in any language — none of the three databases consulted lists one, and the post says so rather than inventing a construction.

A grep of strapi-live-articles.json (905 live articles) for sign / deaf / asl in the slug returns only birthday-banner, sign-in-sheet and design-page slugs — no signed-language article exists on the site. What this post adds to the hub is the one signed entry: a language family the hub does not cover at all, with database codes, phonological parameters and the honest refusal to print what cannot be sourced. No merge is recommended and no line of the hub's table is restated.

THE THREE MANDATORY FIRST-PARTY CAVEATS APPEAR IN BODY PROSE. (1) n = 214 over the two months since the template went live on 2026-07-28, "too short for a seasonal claim, too small for a per-city rate" — stated in the sentence introducing the comparison table. (2) The 2,417 recorded views are page views, not unique visitors, with the twenty-reopens example — stated in the closing section. (3) The 47 city pairs come from a 15-city picker with a default and describe the picker as much as the senders; the genuinely sender-chosen fields are named in the same paragraph — also in the closing section.

SERP RUN, NOT PREDICTED — AND THE ENGINE'S OWN SYNTHESIS WAS WRONG ABOUT BSL. One WebSearch on the exact keyword on 2026-09-25 returned ten results: a jewellery retailer's "Ultimate Guide" post (www2.parklanejewelry.com), aslbloom.com, signingsavvy.com, lifeprint.com, lead-academy.org, handspeak.com, a Facebook group post, a Pinterest pin, pocketsign.org and signlanguage-translator.com. No AI Overview or featured snippet was returned. No university, government body, lexical database or peer-reviewed work appears anywhere on page one; asl-lex.org, bslsignbank.ucl.ac.uk and islrtc.nic.in are all absent. None was linked, cited or paraphrased. The synthesis generated from those pages gave a single ASL recipe and a single BSL recipe without ever asking which language was meant, and asserted for BSL "place two fingers on your throat while signing miss" — BSL SignBank's two entries for miss mean disappoint and mistake, and neither means longing. That mis-answer is the gap this post fills.

SOURCES THAT COULD NOT BE READ, RECORDED RATHER THAN HIDDEN. link.springer.com (ASL-LEX 1.0, Behavior Research Methods, doi 10.3758/s13428-016-0742-0), academic.oup.com (ASL-LEX 2.0, Journal of Deaf Studies and Deaf Education 26(2):263–277, doi 10.1093/deafed/enaa038) and degruyterbrill.com (SignGram Blueprint, doi 10.1515/9781501511806) all returned bot challenges — "Client Challenge", HTTP 403 and "verify that you're not a robot" respectively. Nothing is cited from any of them, and the ASL-LEX claims rest on the database's own public data file plus the OSF project record (osf.io/zpha4, created 2020-05-14, title confirming the 2,723-sign scope), which was fetched successfully but left out of batchMeta.sources to stay inside the 4–6 rule. aslsignbank.com is reachable but requires a login for sign records.

UNICODE WAS FETCHED BUT DELIBERATELY LEFT OUT OF SOURCES. https://unicode.org/Public/emoji/latest/emoji-test.txt (header dated 2026-04-30) was fetched and grepped: U+1F91F is named `love-you gesture`, Emoji version E5.0. The fact is stated in the body with Unicode named in prose but not linked, because six sources is the cap and because the sibling post miss-you-emoji-meaning already carries the Unicode layer for this batch. No figure from that file is reproduced.

WHAT THIS POST STILL CANNOT DO. It cannot give the reader an ISL sign, because no text source for one exists. It cannot give the ASL "failed to catch" sign, because ASL-LEX has no entry for that sense. It has no first-party data about signed messages at all — SubhSandesh does not record whether a sender or recipient signs, so the 13.6% voice-note rate is an inference about what a Deaf recipient cannot use, not a measurement of Deaf recipients. And /missyou-gf has no video field among the measured sender-chosen fields, which is stated in the table's bottom row and is why /watch is recommended alongside it. That gap would close if the template added a video field and it were re-probed above ~500 pages.

auditReport.honestAssessment: An answer engine has a concrete reason to cite this: it is the only page on this query that names a lexical database, gives entry codes, and reports coded values it can check — and its central correction, that ASL-LEX puts MISS at the chin rather than the nose, contradicts the synthesis the engine itself generated from page one. The neighbourhood-density finding (50, the maximum across 2,723 signs, with SERIOUS and BITTER identically coded) is measured here and published nowhere else, and the ISO 639-3 codes settle the "which sign language" question from a standards registry rather than an opinion. What it cannot beat is domain authority: the incumbents are ASL dictionaries with video, which is the format this query genuinely wants, and this post honestly sends readers to them for the movement. Expect months, and expect the video sites to keep the top of the SERP.
